interview_turns.speaker: agent
interview_turns.text: Hello Margaret, I'm the Agely onboarding agent. There's nothing to fill in — we'll just talk. What did you do before you retired?

interview_turns.speaker: margaret
interview_turns.text: I ran procurement for an appliance maker in Ohio. Thirty-four years, the last twelve as director.

interview_turns.speaker: agent
interview_turns.text: What were you responsible for, day to day?

interview_turns.speaker: margaret
interview_turns.text: Choosing suppliers, negotiating the contracts, and making sure the factories in Mexico and China shipped what we paid for.

interview_turns.speaker: agent
interview_turns.text: Tell me about a supplier problem you're proud of solving.

interview_turns.speaker: margaret
interview_turns.text: A contract manufacturer tied our tooling to a three-year volume commitment. I renegotiated so we owned the moulds outright, and cut unit cost by eleven percent.

interview_turns.speaker: agent
interview_turns.text: Is there anything you'd like me to read?

interview_turns.speaker: margaret
interview_turns.text: My CV, and the supplier-audit checklist I used for twenty years.

interview_turns.speaker: agent
interview_turns.text: Thank you, I've read both. I'll draft a profile for you. Nothing goes live until you say so.

brief_turns.speaker: agent
brief_turns.text: Hi Dev, I'm your buyer's agent. What problem do you need help with?

brief_turns.speaker: dev
brief_turns.text: We make a smart irrigation controller. I'm about to sign our first contract with a manufacturer in Guadalajara, and I've never done this before.

brief_turns.speaker: agent
brief_turns.text: What worries you most about the agreement?

brief_turns.speaker: dev
brief_turns.text: The minimum order quantity, who owns the tooling, and what happens if units arrive faulty.

brief_turns.speaker: agent
brief_turns.text: How much time do you need, and what's your budget?

brief_turns.speaker: dev
brief_turns.text: Thirty minutes would do. Somewhere between fifty and a hundred dollars per fifteen minutes.

brief_turns.speaker: agent
brief_turns.text: Got it. I've drafted a brief for you to check.

brief.problem: Review the commercial terms of my first contract-manufacturing agreement before I sign.

debrief_turns.speaker: agent
debrief_turns.text: How did the session with Dev go?

debrief_turns.speaker: margaret
debrief_turns.text: Well. He hadn't noticed the tooling clause — the manufacturer kept ownership of the moulds.

debrief_turns.speaker: agent
debrief_turns.text: What do you always ask first when you read one of these agreements?

debrief_turns.speaker: margaret
debrief_turns.text: What's the minimum order, who owns the tooling, and when do they get paid.

debrief_turns.speaker: agent
debrief_turns.text: And what do you check before you'd call it safe to sign?

debrief_turns.speaker: margaret
debrief_turns.text: That acceptance criteria are written down, that prices can't rise without notice, and that tooling transfers if you leave.

debrief_turns.speaker: agent
debrief_turns.text: I've turned that into a workflow for your engine. Nothing is added until you approve it.

workflow.name: First read of a contract-manufacturing agreement
questions: What is the minimum order quantity, and is it per order or per year?
Who owns the tooling and moulds?
When and how does the manufacturer get paid?
checks: Acceptance criteria (sampling and defect limits) are written into the agreement
Price increases need notice and have a cap
Tooling and designs transfer to you if you leave
watchOuts: A minimum order with no limit on the total commitment
Tooling held hostage to volume commitments
